title: How a study gets made
summary: Every replication goes through the same five steps, and every repository is laid out the same way, so a reader always knows where to look.

blocks.body:
A replication is only worth reading if someone else can check it. I treat each one like a small paper with its working shown: the question, the data, the code, the results, and a list of what the study cannot tell you.

The {replications} replications on this site were all built this way.

items.title: Pick the paper
items.text: The reading list comes from a bibliography of {papers} papers on monopoly and market power. 610 of them are marked as must-reads and ordered into a 14-phase reading plan. I work through it and choose papers whose central claim can be tested again.

items.title: Read it closely
items.text: Before any code, I write a methods review: what the paper claims, which result I am going to test, what I actually read, and what the original numbers were.

items.title: Find public data
items.text: Everything is rebuilt from sources anyone can download: Census tables, FRED series, SEC filings, Medicare records. The raw files sit in the repository next to the code that reads them.

items.title: Rebuild, then extend
items.text: First reproduce the original result as closely as the public data allows. Then run the same test on the years the authors never saw. Tables, figures and the full list of findings are saved to `results/`.

items.title: Write it for a reader
items.text: The write-up opens with a real example, explains the idea without jargon, reports the numbers, and ends with two sections: why it matters, and the limits of the study. A separate technical companion holds the data notes, test statistics and steps to reproduce everything.
